claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions alter electron-phonon coupling through variations in electronic density.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a random distribution of several principal metallic elements and inherent chemical disorder.
Systematic annealing or mechanical processing can produce controlled reductions or enhancements in residual lattice strain.
Local lattice distortions modify electron density.
Distortion-induced changes in electron density modulate the strength of electron-phonon coupling.
Reduced lattice strain produces more spatially uniform electron-phonon coupling.
Reduced lattice strain strengthens electron-phonon coupling.
Stronger and more uniform electron-phonon coupling increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Reduced lattice strain narrows the superconducting transition.
Enhanced lattice strain disrupts electron-phonon coupling.
For otherwise compositionally identical samples, the sample with minimized lattice strain will have a higher transition temperature than a high-strain or as-cast sample.
For otherwise compositionally identical samples, the sample with minimized lattice strain will have a sharper superconducting transition than a high-strain or as-cast sample.
The proposed relationship is limited to high-entropy alloys whose superconductivity is predominantly electron-phonon mediated.
The proposed relationship may not apply when magnetic fluctuations or unconventional pairing mechanisms dominate superconductivity.
Electron correlation and elemental-valence variations could also influence superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
